analysis.one_liner: Requires high-risk chemical plants to assess attack and release risks, plan security measures, and consider safer technologies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in two House committees and their subcommittees until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the EPA to identify chemical facilities that pose the greatest danger if attacked or sabotaged, and to require their owners to assess their vulnerability, write prevention and emergency-response plans, and consider changing processes to use less dangerous chemicals. It created a public clearinghouse on safer technologies, a fund to help financially strapped plants make those changes, and grants to train workers and first responders. It attached civil and criminal penalties for facilities that defied compliance orders. It was referred to two House committees, sent to subcommittees, and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or attend school near large chemical facilities, water treatment plants, and other sites holding dangerous chemicals, who face the risk of a toxic release from a terrorist attack, theft, or sabotage. Workers at those facilities and firefighters and emergency medical personnel would also benefit from federally funded training in hazard reduction and emergency response.

how_it_helps.text: The EPA would have had to designate high-priority combinations of chemical facilities and dangerous substances based on the severity of harm a release could cause, proximity to population centers, and threats to national security [S2][S3].

Owners and operators of those facilities would have to assess their vulnerability to terrorist attack or other unauthorized release, identify hazards, and file prevention, preparedness, and response plans, including goals for shrinking the zone that could be harmed by a release and evaluating evacuation plans for nearby residents [S2][S3].

Plans would have had to consider safer design and maintenance, including inherently safer technology such as using less hazardous substances, storing smaller quantities, and creating buffer zones between facilities and homes, schools, and hospitals [S3].

The bill created a public clearinghouse on safer technologies, a Technology Transition Fund to help facilities in financial hardship adopt them, and grants to train first responders and plant workers in hazard reduction and emergency response [S2][S3].
Facilities that ignored compliance orders faced civil penalties up to $25,000 per day and criminal fines and possible imprisonment for knowing violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical facility owners and operators, who would bear the cost of vulnerability assessments, security measures, planning, and potentially switching to safer processes; federal taxpayers would fund the grants and administration. Facilities could pass some compliance costs on through higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be costly for facility operators, particularly assessments, security upgrades, and any redesign of production processes to use inherently safer technology; the bill acknowledges this by offering hardship grants from a Technology Transition Fund, but those grants would draw on unspecified Treasury funds with no dollar cap [S3].

The vulnerability assessments and plans submitted to the government describe exactly how a plant could be attacked or sabotaged; the bill tries to manage this by exempting the documents from public disclosure and requiring the EPA to develop security protocols, but critics of such regimes have long warned that any collection of this information creates a new target for leaks or misuse [S3].

The bill's mandate to consider inherently safer technology would push some facilities toward process changes whose costs and feasibility vary widely, and the authorization of appropriations was open-ended ('such sums as are necessary') rather than budgeted [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is protection against a low-probability but potentially catastrophic event: a toxic release in a populated area from an attack or theft. The main costs fall on facility operators, softened by hardship grants, and the most serious design weakness is the open-ended funding and the challenge of keeping sensitive assessments out of hostile hands. On balance, this is a conventional preventive regulatory bill whose costs are modest relative to the harm it aims to prevent, but the threat it addresses is contingent rather than everyday.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on introduction day, then split between subcommittees a week later, and that is where it stopped: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ) introduced the bill on May 10, 2005, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Homeland Security Committee [S1][S5].
Ten House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors are listed [S4].

On May 19 it was referred to the Homeland Security Subcommittee on Economic Security, Infrastructure Protection, and Cybersecurity, and on May 23 to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials [S5].
Pallone delivered introductory remarks on the measure four times between May 17 and June 15, 2005, and the record shows no further action after June 15, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical facility operators are better off: they never faced the mandatory vulnerability assessments, planning requirements, penalties, or potential process-change pressures this bill would have imposed. Nearby residents never gained the protections either.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 10, 2005, sent it to the Environment and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee on May 23, and took no further action on it.

against.name: Chemical industry
against.role: Facility owners and operators who would bear the bill's compliance costs
against.what_they_did: The industry lobby opposed mandatory federal chemical security requirements, particularly any requirement to consider inherently safer technologies, and favored a voluntary approach during the mid-2000s chemical security debates.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — the sponsor plus 10 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans listed — but there was never a floor vote, so the partisan split shows only in sponsorship, not in any recorded tally.

industries.note: Facilities holding dangerous chemicals would face mandatory vulnerability assessments, security and planning requirements, EPA compliance orders, and fines up to $25,000 per day, plus potential pressure to redesign processes around safer technologies. Operators' interest in avoiding those costs ran against the bill's aim of protecting nearby communities from a toxic release.

Water treatment plants storing chlorine and other hazardous substances fall under the Clean Air Act definition of stationary sources the bill draws on, so large urban utilities would have been swept into the assessment and planning regime and its costs, while gaining the same federal threat information and hardship grants as industrial plants.

industries.industry: Safety and security equipment and consulting providers
industries.note: The bill's required security measures — intrusion detection sensors, access controls, computer network security — and its assessment and planning mandates would have created demand for security vendors and safety consultants serving covered facilities.

industries.industry: Worker safety and first responder training organizations
industries.note: The bill funded grants, administered possibly through the National Institute for Environmental Health Sciences, to nonprofit organizations with experience in worker health and safety or first responder training programs.
